title: Teaching Tragedy in Tragic Times: Relying on Dante and Aristotle
author: Christine Norvell
summary: Christine Norvell, a literature teacher whose students know loss from floods, fires, tornadoes, and car wrecks, asks how educators should treat real tragedy while teaching tragedy as a literary form. She notes that a newspaper piece offered only two postures, the classroom as haven or the classroom as analytic debate, and finds both thin. She proposes a prepared response: deciding ahead of time how she will look at tragic circumstances, much as a new teacher must decide how to handle discipline. Turning to the tradition, she contrasts Dante's medieval definition, which measures comedy and tragedy by whether a life ends in hope of eternity, with Aristotle's Poetics, where tragedy imitates action and hamartia means a good person missing a high mark rather than a character flaw. She argues that student-help summaries flatten these ideas into a bulleted list and that recovering the fuller account lets students see suffering with dignity and shared humanity.
points: Teachers are not trained counselors, but as humanities teachers they know tragedy better than their students' hearts, and that knowledge is a resource for responding to grief.
A prepared response, deciding in advance how one will view tragic circumstances, is as necessary for tragedy as it is for classroom discipline.
Dante defined comedy and tragedy by perspective: a life with suffering can still be comic if it ends in the hope of eternity.
Aristotle's hamartia is a good person aiming at something exceptionally high and missing, not a moral flaw, and tragedy need not end in death.
Seeing a great soul in pain should transform our concepts of pain and death by showing the dignity of human life and its capacity to endure.
quotes: I had to know how I look at tragic circumstances, to consciously think of it. In the world of psychology, this practice is known as prepared response, to anticipate how we hope to respond to a negative situation.
As much as we care for our students, we are not trained counselors, especially as we encounter grief and pain.
We teach tragedies and likely know them better than we do the hearts of the individuals in the seats in front of us. And that uniquely is where I think part of the answer lies.
Twentieth century tragedies often reflect a lack of perspective, a lack of an eternal view. My students see this quite easily.
A bulleted list, nice graphics, and tragedy in a nutshell. No mention of fate or the role of the gods or any concept of a greater or eternal perspective.
Unfortunately, many students are unaware that the Greek term “hamartia” does not mean flaw at all or even “missing the mark.
It is a good person attempting to do something admirable, and yet they miss. Few students however are aware of this context or the carefully crafted nature of the Greek tragic hero.

Seeing a great soul in pain or death should transform these concepts of pain and death for us because tragedy involves the dignity and significance of human life, and often, man’s ability to endure suffering.
